_comment: Storyboard for the unit lecture film of Marking Out and Cutting a Halving Joint (Professor Adow TVET, Carpentry Tools & Joints). One BEAT is one narration clip and one drawing state: the animation is timed from the MEASURED length of each clip, so a line appears exactly as it is named rather than on a guessed schedule — that is what `art.at` is for, each mark keyed to the phrase in the narration that calls it. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. Unlike the Science films this one lifts nothing out of a lesson kit: the carpentry drawings live in the app as SVG DOM and the film engine emits SVG strings at a given time, so every picture is drawn fresh in film-scenes/adow-carpentry/halving-joint.js. The learner is an adult at grade 8-11 level; the narration is a tradesperson explaining a job, not a teacher addressing a child.
title: Marking Out and Cutting a Halving Joint
subtitle: Carpentry Tools & Joints

brand.name: Professor Adow TVET
brand.by: A short unit lecture from Professor Adow TVET

objectives: Work from the face side and face edge for every measurement, and never from a damaged or unprepared end.
Square a shoulder line across the face and down both edges with a try square, continuing the line without stepping.
Set a marking gauge to a stated dimension and gauge the cheek lines from the face side on both members.
Mark the waste clearly on the correct side of every line before any cut is made.
Saw on the waste side of the line, leaving the line on the work.
Dry-fit a joint before glue is applied and correct the fit rather than forcing it.

scenes.heading: Marking Out and Cutting a Halving Joint

beats.say: Two pieces of timber have to cross, and finish flush. This is how that is done.
A halving joint. Each member loses exactly half its thickness where they meet.
Take half off one, half off the other, and the two faces come together level. That is the whole idea, and everything else is accuracy.
Three tools do this job. A try square, to prove a line square.
A marking gauge, to score the same distance from a face every time.
And a tenon saw: fine teeth for a clean cut across the grain, and a stiff back that keeps the cut straight.
Start with a prepared piece. Planed straight, planed square, gauged to size.
One wide face is marked as the face side. One edge, square to it, is marked as the face edge.
Every measurement from here comes off those two surfaces. Not off a sawn end, and not off whichever side is nearest.

at.no: not off whichever side is nearest

beats.say: Take the width from the piece that has to fit, not from the drawing.
Square the shoulder line across the face, and down both edges. The stock of the square presses hard against the face edge.
If the stock lifts even slightly, the line is not square, and neither is anything you cut to it.
Set the gauge to half the thickness. Lock it, then measure it again before it touches the wood.
Score the cheek line with the fence riding on the face side, on both members, from the one setting.
One setting used twice keeps the halves equal. A gauge a millimetre out puts the joint two millimetres out, because the error lands on both.
Now hatch the waste. This is the last mark before the first cut that cannot be undone.
It takes seconds, and it is why nobody who does it ever saws off the wrong half.
The saw takes out a kerf about a millimetre wide. That millimetre has to come out of the waste.

at.kerf: a kerf about a millimetre wide

beats.say: Saw on the waste side and the line stays on the work. The joint is full size, and a shaving brings it home.
Saw down the middle of the line and half the kerf comes out of the joint. It is slack, and nothing puts wood back.

at.bad: down the middle of the line

beats.say: Pare the waste with a chisel, cutting from both faces towards the middle, so the far edge is supported and does not tear out.
Then fit it dry. If it needs a mallet it is too tight: take a shaving off the cheek and try it again.
It should go together by hand and stay there. Check both diagonals before any glue.
Face side and face edge. Shoulder squared, cheek gauged, waste hatched.
Sawn on the waste side, pared to the line, fitted dry. In that order, every time.
